title: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Nigel Farage tells BBC
description: Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's funding.Speaking to the BBC ah
body: Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's funding.Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and £5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.Farage said he expects it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed as part of the ongoing parliamentary investigation into whether he should have publicly declared the sum upon his election as an MP.The Reform UK leader said he hoped the investigation, which was launched in May but paused during the by-election he triggered in his Clacton seat, would "move a bit faster" now he had been re-elected to Parliament.Farage has faced weeks of headlines about funding, including £5m he received before entering Parliament from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based British cryptocurrency investor and major Reform donor.Parliament's standards commissioner is investigating whether he should have declared that sum upon becoming an MP in his published register of financial interests.Farage has said the £5m was a personal gift and did not therefore require registration under the rules. He continued to insist he believes he had done "nothing wrong", but ultimately it would be a "matter of interpretation" for the investigation to resolve. Asked about the funding questions that have dogged the party over the summer recess, he said: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society. "If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do"."There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat."There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing."So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour. "People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything." Elsewhere in his interview, Farage acknowledged that Reform was "down a bit" in its poll ratings compared to 2025, after failing to win in by-elections this year including Gorton and Denton and Makerfield, which saw Andy Burnham's re-election as an MP ahead of becoming Labour leader. But he added that "markets don't move in straight lines," adding that the party still had "every chance" of winning the next general election, due by 2029.He said the party was continuing to look "outside of the political sphere" to fill frontbench positions, following a raft of appointments earlier this year to senior posts within the party.And he said he continued to hold to his previous prediction there would be an election next spring "forced on the government" by the markets, amid rising costs to public borrowing.Reform's conference, he said, would be a chance for the party to set out details of the "fundamental changes" it would make within 100 days of winning power, adding that voters were more interested in who is "actually going to deliver" than the specifics of individual policies.

schema.headline: Reform up against 'complainants' society', Nigel Farage tells BBC

title: Jurors return in Lindsay Clancy trial after judge asks them to break deadlock
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC inside court as jury in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlockedByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdated 44 minutes a
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC inside court as jury in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlockedByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdated 44 minutes agoThe jury in the US trial of Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Wednesday to try again to reach a verdict in the deaths of her three children.The panel had told the judge a day earlier they had been unable to agree after days of deliberations and were instructed to keep trying. Clancy, who has pleaded not guilty, faces three counts of first-degree murder.Prosecutors have alleged that she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill the children in their Massachusetts home in 2023. Her lawyer does not dispute Clancy killed them but says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was unable to distinguish right from wrong - meaning she should not be held criminally responsible.The jury began deliberating on Thursday after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. The panel returned to the courtroom on Tuesday, after telling Judge William Sullivan they were deadlocked. The announcement drew audible gasps in the courtroom. He instructed them to keep trying.Clancy, a 36-year-old former nurse, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer. She was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window after the killings.It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations.A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC.Although jurors have not been provided a specific deadline, there is a limitation to the number of times that a judge is expected to ask them to continue deliberating. If they say a second time that they are at an impasse, the judge has a new recourse."If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said.But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.If the jury reports that it is deadlocked for a third time, the judge could declare a mistrial.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Clancy in court on TuesdayCriminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC she was not surprised to hear that the jury was deadlocked, as people had strong opinions on the case."The facts are difficult and a lot of the evidence is graphic so they have a lot weighing on them," she said.The five-week trial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, has generated significant public interest and crowds have sometimes gathered outside as hearings take place. A woman was arrested on Tuesday by state police outside the court building, Massachusetts State Police confirmed to the BBC. She was expected to be charged on Wednesday with "intimidation of a witness, jurors, or person furnishing information". Police did not give any further information, and it was not clear whether the incident was connected to the Clancy trial. Image source, Plymouth Clerks OfficeImage caption, Clancy family picture exhibited in courtClancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home in January 2023. The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis - a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth - and that for this reason she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings.If she is found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars.If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed.  She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide: www.befrienders.org, external.In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

title: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death
description: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn -
body: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, having suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield, appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court alongside Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37, and Peter Horvath, 38, all of Holywell Heights.They have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also appeared in the same court charged with perverting the course of justice.All five Slovakian nationals were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday. Tuesday's hearing was told the baby's body was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse and was wrapped in a towel inside a blue bag.Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson said the defendants had been accused of perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene.Earlier, police said two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remained on bail.Speaking ahead of the court hearing, Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl."I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation."We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course."Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries. Listen to highlights from South Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North

title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine."That's a secret. A military secret."Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.And that, I suspect, is the point.Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe. Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport. Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks."If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine. Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure."I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war"."War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys."We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
description: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig
body: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport."We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil"."We will not tolerate it," she said.While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole."We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.High-voltage power lines were damaged near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at Skarżysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and children in Ukraine".

schema.headline: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig

title: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night
description: It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs. The markets lending money to
body: It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs. The markets lending money to governments appear to be changing more fundamentally too.Over summer, the message has been made clear: countries will have to pay more to borrow cash.The immediate reason is the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, which has pushed up inflation and, in turn, raised expectations of higher interest rates in the world's major economies.Markets had assumed tensions would subside, and so too would oil and gas prices, ahead of the US midterm elections in November.It was wishful thinking, based on the hope that US President Donald Trump would want the conflict in the Middle East resolved well before Americans go to the polls. But that has not happened, leaving markets pricing in higher energy prices, a chronic Gulf crisis, higher inflation for longer - and so higher interest rates.But that is only part of the story.The bigger picture is rising demand for borrowing across the world - and not just from governments. Big tech companies are turning to the same bond markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars for investments in AI data centres.Over $219bn (£162bn) of debt has already been issued this year by the US "hyperscalers" such as Google, Amazon and Meta, nearly a third of it in currencies other than the dollar, including sterling.The total issued last year was $93bn, while before that it averaged less than $40bn a year. Some expect the tech giants to raise $400-$500bn from the bond markets this year. These are staggering sums, raising competition in the market and pushing up the price for governments.Looking east, there is another major borrower: Japan.It has the highest debt burden, relative to its GDP, of the major economies and is the biggest single lender to the US government. Until recently its central bank's interest rate was zero, but that has crept up to help combat rising inflation. As a result, its government bond yields have been pushed to 30-year highs. The declining value of the yen complicates things, but the bottom line is that there is a change afoot in the global flow of money.The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt". But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor. Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike. Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans."More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night

title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
description: Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, cl
body: Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country.His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham.But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending.Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline.He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs.David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box.But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone.The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few -  hurtling towards him.These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

schema.headline: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics

title: Why are bond yields rising and how does it affect me?
description: The government's ability to play with the public finances is limited by the so-called fiscal rules it has set for itself.  So, if it needs more money
body: The government's ability to play with the public finances is limited by the so-called fiscal rules it has set for itself.  So, if it needs more money to pay back higher borrowing costs, it has less to spend on other things (under its self-imposed rules).The possibility now looms of less support for households struggling with the cost of living, or of tax rises to pay for any support.Importantly, these are choices – not certainties – so the chancellor might free up some money by spending less elsewhere.Some may be wondering about the impact of higher gilt yields on the mortgage market, particularly after what followed Liz Truss's mini-Budget in September 2022.Analysts believe that mortgage rates could go up on new fixed deals, as funding costs for lenders rise. But this is very different to 2022, when they shot up over a couple of days. That speedy rise led to lenders quickly pulling deals while they tried to work out what interest rate to charge.However, the market could be more favourable to anyone currently buying an annuity - a product from an insurance company that gives a retirement income for the rest of their life, bought only once.

schema.headline: Why are bond yields rising and how does it affect me?

title: Kids eat free and loyalty points - six ways to eat out but not break the bank
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter The price of eating out can be hard to swallow while the cost of living remains high, with mor
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter The price of eating out can be hard to swallow while the cost of living remains high, with more than a third of Brits cutting back on going to restaurants, according to YouGov's latest Dining Out report., externalRestaurateurs say the rising cost of food, energy, wage and tax bills mean they've had to put up prices, with some top chefs campaigning for government help. Many eateries are offering incentives to get diners through the doors. Here are some ways to save money on meals out.1. Eat and repeatMany restaurants offer points, freebies, discounts and birthday treats to keep customers coming back. One of the most well-known is the Pizza Express Club. Regular diners can progress through a bronze, silver and gold system unlocking perks from free dough balls to hot and soft drinks on the house.Nando's uses a chilli system for its loyalty programme, while other schemes such as Tastecard offer discounts at hundreds of eat-in and takeaway venues in exchange for an annual fee.2. Go early - or lateRestaurants often want to fill seats outside of peak lunch and dinner hours so opting for earlier or later sittings can be rewarded by a cheaper bill.Apps such as First Table, which operates across 21 UK cities, as well as Ireland, New Zealand and Australia, give diners 50% off food when they book a participating restaurant's first or last dining slot. In exchange, diners pay a small booking fee. EatClub is another, giving walk-ins up to 50% off the whole bill at thousands of venues when they redeem an offer within its app. The biggest discounts are at off-peak times.Shokofeh Hejazi, director of foresight and innovation at global trends agency The Food People, says earlier dining appeals because it tends to be quieter and calmer, people drink less and it allows them to get home sooner. Meeting up for breakfast also tends to be a bit more wallet-friendly as it's usually just one course and diners get the same catch-up time with friends and family, she adds. 3. Kids eat freeIn the school holidays, many places will entice families through their doors by offering free or £1 meals for kids eating with paying adults.These range from big chains such as TGI Fridays, cafes at supermarkets including Morrisons and Asda, and even garden centres like Dobbies.While some tie-in with school holidays, other deals are all year round.4. Hit up soft launchesMany new restaurants will offer discounts in a bid to encourage diners to try them out and spread the word that they've opened for business. These are known as "soft launches" and can run for several weeks. They're a cost-effective way of trying a higher-end restaurant without such a hit to the wallet.Keep track by signing up to newsletters that list upcoming openings in the local area. Hejazi says some restaurants are extending the period before they fully open to garner more buzz, while others are making their soft launch pricing permanent for quieter days such as Mondays. People shouldn't assume they're priced out of fine dining-type venues because "there's access points for everybody in a lot of these places", she says.5. Make your supermarket points work harderSupermarket loyalty points from those weekly shops add up over time so why not put them toward a meal out? For example, each 50p earned in Tesco Clubcard points can be exchanged £1.50 in vouchers to spend at participating Prezzo Italian venues. The chain is just one of Tesco's restaurant partners.6. Surplus food appsFinally, there are plenty of options to take away food for free or at a fraction of the usual price.Surplus food apps such as Too Good To Go, or Olio, allow customers to bag goodies that would otherwise go to waste.It's a bit of a gamble - you don't always know precisely what you'll be getting.But there's money to be saved on items needed to buy anyway, that's more cash left over for when you do decide to dine out.Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: Kids eat free and loyalty points - six ways to eat out but not break the bank

title: Early release scheme set to free 2,500 prisoners by end of year
description: About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of th
body: About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying"."I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded. The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:From 10 November, 650 offenders serving up to three years and two monthsFrom 8 December, 550 offenders serving up to four years and three monthsFrom 12 January 2027, 600 offenders serving up to five years and nine monthsFrom 9 February, 500 offenders serving up to seven years and six monthsFrom 9 March, 200 offenders serving up to nine yearsFrom 13 April, 200 offenders serving up to 10 yearsFrom 11 May, 250 offenders serving up to 12 yearsFrom 9 June, 250 offenders serving more than 12 years.The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.Under the new rules this group will instead leave jail at the halfway point.The ministerial order lists all of the 71 crimes that are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, and sexual and grooming offences.Prisoners on a special form of extended sentence and those on life terms are excluded from the scheme.On Tuesday, the government explained it was creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.An investment of £110m, which is set to come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.Justice Secretary Alex Norris told the BBC being released did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.Norris also said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

schema.headline: Early release scheme set to free 2,500 prisoners by end of year

title: Tiger Woods gets five-year driving ban after reckless driving plea
description: "I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case," Florida  State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said at a press conference after
body: "I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case," Florida  State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said at a press conference after the hearing.He said he strove to treat Woods like any other defendant."Today I resolved case involving a man who drives a golf ball for a living," Bakkedahl said. "Tomorrow, I'll resolve a case in the same matter for a man who drives a nail for a living."No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom". He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning. He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today."I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

schema.headline: Tiger Woods gets five-year driving ban after reckless driving plea

title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
description: Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn
body: Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes. "We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine has since formally notified the UN of the risks to civilian aviation.Russian President Vladimir Putin said the comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism". Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia because of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries like Turkey and China do.Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives."There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow.In a statement on X, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Ukraine had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe for civilian aviation."We want to prevent unintended incidents," he said, adding: "The war is returning home to Russia."On Wednesday afternoon, flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed many planes flying over Russia, including arriving and departing from the two main airports.Several airlines that fly through Russia told the BBC that they were carefully monitoring the situation.Qatar Airways, which flies into Moscow and travels through Russian airspace to get to the US west coast, said its flight planning was "guided by rigorous and continuous monitoring of airspace security, safety assessments, and geopolitical developments".FlyDubai, an Emirati government-owned carrier, told the BBC that it would "closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary".Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures. Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday.Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption.Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area. Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year."There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists."His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations.The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row.A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from".Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair. Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe.    Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022.Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period.The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board.Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014.The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster.In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed.He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.

schema.headline: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations

title: Buckinghamshire pub's manager stabbed to death in Germany
description: A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local aut
body: A Foreign Office spokesperson told the BBC: "We are supporting the family of a British woman who died in Germany [and] are in touch with the local authorities."The 31-year-old ran the London Marathon in 2022 in aid of the Milton Keynes-based Spinal Injuries Association, having undergone three spinal operations herself.She was also a member of Thame Runners in Oxfordshire, which said it was "deeply saddened" by her death.In July, she and her clubmates were part of the winning women's team at the Waddesdon 5k in Buckinghamshire."She will be remembered with great affection by the many members who knew her, ran alongside her and shared in her love of running," the club said. Tributes were also paid by the joint masters of the "Bicester Hunt with Whaddon Chase", where she was a secretary.They said: "Becca was a vital and much-loved part of our hunt, both as a dedicated secretary and as a dear friend to so many."Her loss is being felt deeply across our entire community, of which she was such an integral part. We extend our heartfelt sympathies to her family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.

title: Paul Pogba, Raheem Sterling & Jamie Vardy among free agents after transfer deadline day
description: The summer transfer window is closed but there are still a host of talented players without a club and therefore available to sign for free.BBC Sport
body: The summer transfer window is closed but there are still a host of talented players without a club and therefore available to sign for free.BBC Sport takes a look at some of the biggest stars who are currently out of contract and up for grabs.Paul Pogba, 33 (Last club: Monaco)Former Manchester United midfielder Pogba has played very little football since his 18 month doping ban ended in March 2025. The Frenchman made just six appearances for Monaco after joining them last summer and, after a series of injuries, the French club terminated his contract last month - one year before it was due to end. Karim Benzema, 38 (Last club: Al Hilal)French striker Benzema has been plying his trade in Saudi Arabia since leaving Real Madrid in 2023, spending three years with Al Ittihad. But just six months after joining Al-Hilal the Ballon d'Or winner has terminated his contract. The arrival of attacking trio Crysencio Summerville, Ollie Watkins and Gabriel Martinelli has perhaps pushed Benzema out and, despite already making three appearances for Al-Hilal this season, his contract was terminated on 31 August.Riyad Mahrez, 35 (Last club: Al Ahli)Another player to have had their contract terminated in the Saudi Pro League is five-time Premier League winner Mahrez. The Algeria winger joined Al Ahli from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 37 goals in 122 appearances in all competitions. Reports suggest he will stay in the Saudi league and is close to joining Al-Shabab.Raheem Sterling, 31 (Last club: Feyenoord)Sterling was released by Feyenoord after just three months and eight games and is set to appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May. Sources told BBC Sport the former Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea winger had faced "an extremely tough couple of years".Philippe Coutinho, 34 (Last club: Vasco da Gama)Former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder Coutinho left his boyhood club Vasco de Gama in February, saying he was "tired mentally". The Brazilian has not officially announced his retirement and has previously been linked with a move to the MLS. Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly agreed a move to Brazilian club Palmeiras.Dani Carvajal, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)Widely regarded as one of the best right-backs of his generation, Carvajal has been a free agent since his contract with Real Madrid ended in June. Carvajal made 451 appearances across all competitions for Real in 13 years and has not been linked with a new club. He has reportedly been training at the Spanish Football Federation's facilities over the summer with compatriot and fellow free agent Joselu.Jamie Vardy, 39 (Last club: Cremonese)Vardy spent last season with Cremonese after 13 years with Leicester City but relegation to Serie B prompted the Italian side to let the striker go. He has been heavily linked with a move back to the English Football League with Wrexham, Sheffield Wednesday and West Ham all reportedly interested.David Alaba, 34 (Last club: Real Madrid)Experienced full-back Alaba left Real Madrid in May after five years with the club and, for a spell this summer, Manchester United were the bookies' favourite to sign the Austrian. The former Bayern Munich star has had a storied club career that has yielded 12 league titles and four Champions Leagues. Despite speculation of interest from a number of clubs as his Real contract came to an end, so far, Alaba has not signed for anyone.Sergio Ramos, 40 (Last club: Monterrey)Legendary Spanish defender Ramos has been without a club since December 2025 after leaving Mexican side Monterrey. Although aged 40, he has not announced his retirement while some reports suggest he still feels fit enough to compete at a high level. Earlier this year he spearheaded a consortium who attempted to acquire a controlling stake in his former club Sevilla but the bid failed.

schema.headline: Paul Pogba, Raheem Sterling & Jamie Vardy among free agents after transfer deadline day

title: Everton's transfer deadline day debacle leaves owners facing fan mutiny
description: Everton's shambolic end to the transfer window has resulted in open revolt from supporters that places fierce scrutiny on owners The Friedkin Group an
body: Everton's shambolic end to the transfer window has resulted in open revolt from supporters that places fierce scrutiny on owners The Friedkin Group and chief executive Angus Kinnear.The last straw for fans already infuriated by the controversial proposed sale of home-grown youngster Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest - the deal was eventually blocked by Everton's board in the face of the toxic reaction from the fanbase - was the bungled final day before the window closed.Folarin Balogun's proposed £40m move from AS Monaco descended into high farce in the early hours of Wednesday morning after the original deal was renegotiated when issues arose with his medical, ending with the United States striker deciding to walk away from Everton's Finch Farm training base without signing.And all after Balogun, 25, and both clubs had signed the deal sheet allowing the move to be completed after Tuesday's 23.00 BST transfer deadline.Everton had scheduled an 8am flight to bring Balogun to Merseyside, but he was unable to arrive until later in the day. Everton were also frustrated at a delay in receiving documents related to the deal from Monaco.When the problem with his medical cropped up, it prompted Everton to pursue a loan deal for Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee, who was happy to sign but was not allowed to leave Old Trafford. A move was also made for Aston Villa's Tammy Abraham but did not progress as the striker wished to remain at Villa Park.After failing to sign an alternative, a deal was eventually agreed with Monaco, minutes before the deadline, which would have resulted in a smaller up-front payment and a series of triggered payments based on how he progressed. The player's personal terms were unchanged.It was only then that the former Arsenal striker had his change of heart, leaving Finch Farm with Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro telling journalists at a news conference on Wednesday that Balogun was "not comfortable" with how Everton treated him during his medical.Everton believe they supported Balogun throughout the process, while being open about the issues identified. The club also made clear to the player they would work with Monaco to explore a solution that could still enable the transfer to be completed.To make matters worse, and to shed an even more unflattering light on the club's strategy and operation, it all came hours after Everton had sanctioned striker Beto's £15.5m move to Fiorentina.Events unfolded as Everton's most creative player Iliman Ndiaye was completing his £65m move to Manchester City.Everton could point to the fact Balogun took a personal decision they could not reverse, but the bigger question is why they took until the final day of the window to address glaring long-term issues?Kinnear, in what must now be looked upon as an ill-fated recent interview with BBC Radio Merseyside, announced Everton's squad was "in a good place", adding: "The challenge is we want to get the absolute best player we can in their position. Our metric is that by the close of the transfer window we have achieved that."He also relayed the views of Everton's American owners that they regarded missing out on Europe last season as "failure". It was an announcement manager David Moyes admitted came as a "surprise".After the events of recent days, the word "failure" is being applied to the owners and chief executive, not Moyes. And there will be no hiding place for TFG and Kinnear should things now go wrong.The "good place" Kinnear spoke about has eventually amounted to leaving Moyes with just one striker in the raw Thierno Barry and only 18 senior, outfield players, a parlous state of affairs for the 63-year-old Scot, who has at times found it hard to disguise his dissatisfaction with the extent of the summer's transfer business.Everton may have re-signed Jack Grealish on loan, and finally solved a right-back problem stretching back years by signing Ashley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for £3m, but the over-riding verdict on the club's transfer window has to be one of huge embarrassment for TFG and Kinnear.Even the search for a right-back, a problem from last summer and further back, was not smooth, with Maitland-Niles being officially announced shortly after midnight after a £9.4m deal for Fulham's Kenny Tete was shelved when the Cottagers could not find a suitable replacement.As well as only one striker in Barry, Everton's squad now has just one recognised right-back in Maitland-Niles and one left-back in Vitaliy Mykolenko after youngster Adam Aznou was allowed to join Malaga on loan.The last few days have seen one major PR catastrophe narrowly avoided by pulling out of the sale of 19-year-old Armstrong, arguably Everton's most promising academy product since Wayne Rooney, only to walk straight into another, highly damaging one.After the Carabao Cup second-round win at Preston North End, Moyes said: "I still think we have got a lot of work to do. We need more players. Our squad is not big enough and we need to get more quality in some areas if we can do."Moyes' thoughts will be worth much more than a penny, should he choose to air them publicly, while fans' groups have wasted no time in expressing their undisguised anger, with a petition even set up calling for Kinnear's resignation."The Everton Fans' Forum" issued a lengthy statement featuring widescale criticism of the club, saying the Toffees' squad had been left "dangerously short" in key areas.It added: "The conclusion of this summer's transfer window leaves Everton supporters with serious questions about the club's planning, recruitment and decision-making."This is not about demanding that Everton spend recklessly. Supporters understand the financial restrictions the club operates under. We are not demanding marquee signings simply for the sake of it."We are demanding competence, preparation and accountability."And the influential group "The 1878s", volunteers who have created huge flags, banners and tifos to enhance the atmosphere at Everton's new Hill Dickinson Stadium, and whose efforts were described as "unbelievable" by Moyes, has responded to deadline day in similar vein.In a statement it said it is "standing down for the foreseeable future" in protest, saying: "Like the rest of our fanbase, we are utterly disappointed and disgusted with how this transfer window has gone, especially the end of it."Also for fans asking, just to reiterate - when we design flags, there are rules and regulations that we have to adhere to regarding the wording on our flags during displays, we are not allowed derogatory or offensive wording or images."If we were able to get a load of flags in the ground to show our feelings of discontent, disappointment and anger over this whole situation, believe us, we would, but this is something that simply wouldn't be allowed."As well as the last-day signings of Grealish and Maitland-Niles, Everton did make other acquisitions during the window, bringing in PFA Championship Player of the Year Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough. Christian Norgaard was signed from Arsenal - although the 32-year-old Dane is currently injured with no comeback date - as a replacement for departed veteran Idrissa Gueye. Deals for young German Merlin Rohl and England Under-21 winger Tyrique George, on loan last season, were confirmed. Brennan Johnson arrived from Crystal Palace in a straight swap with Dwight McNeil.All this, however, has been overshadowed by a transfer deadline day that ended as nothing short of a debacle. In reality, they have ended this transfer markedly weaker than when they started it.Everton are yet to issue any public statement on the events that have led to such damning criticism, fan rebellion and a loss of credibility for owners TFG - but there are many fences to be mended.If that can be done successfully remains to be seen.

schema.headline: Everton's transfer deadline day debacle leaves owners facing fan mutiny
